utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. We are in the middle of re-examination. The witness should be brought in, please. And then, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to address briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First you should address and then we go into closed session to enable the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I just wanted -- I wanted to address my estimate that I gave yesterday at the end of the day of the length of my re-examination. I did go over the yesterday's transcript and there's three main areas that I'd like to cover with this witness on re-examination. One taking -- going back to where I left off about the region where the minefields were set, the securing of the barracks; then I'd like to discuss -- ask him some questions about the communication facilities as well as the communication with the MUP in the -- in that area; and then, finally, to touch on some of the documents that were -- General Tolimir put to the witness about communications going up to -- from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. Those three areas, I estimate each area will take ten minutes, so, in total, if I could request 30 minutes to complete the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Hopefully we will manage in that time and there's no objection to that. We turn into private session. In fact, into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. And Ms. Hasan is continuing her re-examination. Ms. Hasan, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit P44 displayed on our screens. Page 37 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a single page only document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I assume that you are, in fact, referring to another document which is plain and without markings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. It's 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: P104. We would like to have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Apologies, it's P94. Page 37.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is the photograph of the school we took a look at yesterday, and you identified it as -- that a part of that school -- behind the school was used as a dining hall and a kitchen where your battalion ate their meals. You also testified that behind the school there were some smaller buildings, including the offices of the battalion, as well as a warehouse. Then the logistics security, as well as the logistics platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we turn to page 36 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you take a look at this photograph, this aerial image, the Prosecution has determined through its investigations that that building in the centre of that image is the school that you have identified as having used. Now, if I can just -- actually, at this moment ask the Court Usher to give the witness a pen in order that he may mark this image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the completeness of the record, you're referring to the Konjevic Polje school, aren't you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness said yesterday that his unit, the unit to which he belonged did not use the school. Other forces used the school. However, the Prosecutor just now said that he said that they had used the school. I would like the transcript to reflect accurately what the witness said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Ms. Hasan, in my recollection, it was slightly different what the witness was saying yesterday from what you were putting to him just a moment ago. If I remember correctly, he was referring to buildings behind the school where the little office was situated, where parts of -- where the administration of his unit was located. But you --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where was the dining hall and the kitchen that was used by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we used just one small part behind the school. This is a boiler room that was adapted into a kitchen. And there was a classroom that had its entrance from the top side, and we only used that when there was a large number of soldiers in Konjevic Polje. When there were fewer soldiers, then there was no need for that. It wasn't necessary to cook meals in large quantities, so then the logistics organised itself differently in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you just draw a circle around the part of the building that -- the boiler room that you're referring to where the dining-room was held.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to ask the Prosecutor, if possible, because I see a large blue circle in the centre of this photograph which was not something that the witness marked, so I would like Ms. Hasan to explain what this circle is, and can the transcript reflect that the circle was not drawn in by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think by your remark it is now stated on the record that this was prepared before showing this photograph, aerial image, to the witness. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic, the box to the left, top left of this image, can you tell me what you see there? What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see some buildings at the base of it. And I think that our offices were in this building here that I'm going to mark now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with a 1.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could you please mark the other locations you have marked earlier and put a number 2 next to this earlier marking, in the school building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell me what those buildings below the offices are?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what those buildings were below the offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can give you a closer view of that area?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 1068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this marked aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to come back to this document, but we should mark it as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to tender it as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received with the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit number P1770. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The reason why I ask for that is you will lose the markings if the aerial photograph will be removed without admission. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 1068 displayed on the screen. And, again, just for the record, these markings in yellow are not -- were not made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is a closer view of that box we were just looking at. Does that help you tell me what -- what this depicts?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot see precisely what is shown here. I really can't tell what this is. There are four rectangles.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Our investigations show that these are pontoons that you have previously testified about. And as ...

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not pontoons. Perhaps this is your error. I remember now. We had a set of heavy launcher bridge -- bridges. I think each of them were 10 metres long, each of the vehicles. So that's a total of 40 metres. That's how long this bridge was. The truck that was transporting these launchers was not functioning properly. There had to be some repairs made for the trucks to be -- for the engines to be turned on so that they could be turned in the direction that was ordered. I think these were Karazov [phoen] vehicles. The biggest problem with that, at least this is what the hydraulics craftsmen told us, was that the oil was leaking in the vehicles, and we couldn't keep the oil in there. They had been standing there for too long.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So these vehicles were the property of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were -- belonging to our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May I offer this aerial image as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit number P1771. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could revert back now to P1770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will take a moment to upload it again with the markings of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified about minefields that were on the left and right of the road. Can you show us on this photograph, this aerial image, where the minefields were laid?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that area cannot be seen on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me relative to this area where the minefields were laid?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, this is to the left and to the right of the road that is indicated here. On one side, on the left-hand side, where the school is, and then above the school, there's a small road and a slope, and then that went down towards the road again. And then on this side closer to us, the right side of the road, there was an electricity transmission power line and it went to the guard-post number 6, but it was on that side in the hill. Guard-post number 6 was between the road and the small river. There's a small river here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, sir, the guard post number 6, if I understand you correctly, is it below this road towards the bottom half of this image?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. I cannot indicate it precisely. You can't really see the place in this photograph, But it is below the road. It's between the road and the small river. You can't see the river on the photograph but there is it a small river there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was your battalion defending this entire area that -- from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a system of guard posts and minefields that we had. This was done before we had guard duty up to the minefield and then we also had guard duties at pre-arranged, appointed guard posts. This is something that I didn't do. This was already there before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And these guard posts and minefields, were they there for the purpose of protecting this compound facility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the goal of the guard posts and the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir we -- I showed you a photograph yesterday and we briefly looked at it today which depicts the school as well as the shed. And I mentioned yesterday that there was a witness who was held in that shed in the morning to the afternoon of July 13th, and this would be reference -- would be referenced -- the reference for that is Exhibit P441, the transcript page number is 3253, line 15. This shed that we looked at is in the centre of that light blue circle on this aerial image which seems to be located in the heart of your facilities and the area you were protecting. I'd like to ask you whether you knew that, in that shed or shack, right by that school, close to your offices, close to your dining hall, close to your property, and within your protected area, whether you were aware that there was one -- and actually more people held within that shed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I think your reference can't be correct. Page -- you were referring to page 3253. Yesterday's transcript didn't have this page number. Must be something with 9.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I was actually referring to Exhibit P441, which is the -- which is where the evidence of this witness is contained. And it's from the Krstic trial. And so this is a reference -- the reference I gave is from that trial, which is now -- that transcript is now an exhibit in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give us a reference to the cross-examination of Mr. Tolimir yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The question about the shed and the person held in that shed actually was a question I put to the witness at the beginning of my re-examination. And the basis is to -- to ask the witness about the coordination between the MUP and his battalion, which was -- there was several questions asked about that during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to greet everybody who is present and I would like these proceedings to end in accordance with God's will and not my will. I think that this subject that is currently discussed here, it wasn't simply part of cross-examination. There are no references to my cross-examination and no basis for this re-examination now. I would like the Prosecutor to always mention the reference from my cross-examination. Thank you. This witness never mentioned this house yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, as I indicated yesterday at the end of our hearing, we would really appreciate to give -- to get a reference to the specific part of the cross-examination. If I remember correctly, the cooperation between the unit of the witness and the MUP was part of the examination-in-chief and the questioning by the Chamber. You may check with Mr. McCloskey and your Case Manager, where you will find the reference but we need it, and the -- this must be the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There -- General Tolimir, at page 9504, line 10, asked the witness whether he made any kind of decision or conclusion regarding the cooperation of his unit with the MUP forces. And then subsequently, at line 15, asked whether the person who wrote the 14th July 1995 report for their activities that day, whether that person stated anything about their cooperation with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My problem is that in my e-court system I still have the pages from that day and this was not changed to the ... oh, thank you very much. Page 71, line 1. I'll check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: During cross-examination yesterday, Mr. Tolimir put the following question to the witness -- yesterday's transcript, page 70, line 22: "My question is: In paragraph 8, 'Conclusions, Forecasts and Decisions,' did you make any kind of decision or conclusion regarding the cooperation of your unit with the MUP forces?" "A. I didn't bring -- make any conclusions or issue any orders in relation to cooperation with the MUP." The next question of Mr. Tolimir: "The person you wrote the report for, your activities that day, did they state anything about your cooperation with the MUP? Answer of the witness: "There was nothing else written about cooperation with the MUP other than what is written here." I think now we have a reference, Mr. Tolimir. If you are dealing with that, please carry on, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The references that you mention speak about the contents of the document. It's 65 ter 0284. The witness said that he didn't do anything about it. He gave a negative answer to both my questions. He never mentioned the minefield, the prisoners, the people being kept there or anything like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is the right of the Prosecution during re-examination to challenge this statement of the witness, that he doesn't know anything about that, and Ms. Hasan is dealing with that now. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic, I'll repeat my question, which is: Were you aware, did you learn anything about a person and other persons who were held in this shed on the 13th of July, which is located in the middle of your facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to correct you. This shed was not in the middle of our facilities. I said that we never entered the school. We did not know who was in the school, when, how, or what was the system of exchange of the people therein. We had nothing to do with the school or the access to the school. That's how I found the situation when I came there. There was only one police check-point at the intersection in Konjevic Polje, and they were guarding the lower part of the minefield. I couldn't have known anything about what was going on there because, as I have already stated yesterday, on the 13th, when two of my soldiers were wounded, I wasn't there. I returned only later. I was most probably in Vlasenica at the construction sites. I returned later. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But, sir, you knew who was there. You told us yesterday at page 9515, line 19, 18, you said: "It's the first time I hear that, because we were not using these premises at all. The police were there, those who came and who had shifts there and at the check-points. We were not using these premises at all." So you were aware that the police was there.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I didn't know. I assumed it because of their uniforms and other things. And that's why I said that. I did not cooperate with them. I did not have any contact with them. So I couldn't have known what they were doing, when they were doing it, how they were doing it, and what was their system of shift exchange. It was the police. They had their own organs, their own commands, and they did not belong to the army. Indeed, I have already stated that the police and the army did not have good relations because the police was better supported and had better logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a record of an intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This intercept is under seal. So if it may not be broadcast. Could we have Exhibit P2921A. Apologies, that's a 65 ter number. The P number would be 1538A.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is an intercepted conversation from 7.40 in the morning of the 12th of July, 1995. It's a conversation between an unidentified person and someone identified as "O." And it reads, the unidentified person says: "Obrenovic, O, we don't have any communication there recorded. The unidentified person asks: "Where is your commander?" O responds: "As far as I know, he's here. He's not -- the unidentified person replies: "He's not, he isn't answering. Listen, please tell him that I called. That Mane, Laco's deputy, will call him, that the police in Konjevic Polje have been told to the same as the Engineering Battalion are doing, and that he can give orders to them through the commander of the Engineering Battalion." "Okay." "That's it. Take care." Sir, can you tell me what this is talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear this and that I see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It refers here that the orders to the police located in Konjevic Polje can go through the commander of the Engineering Battalion. And according to your testimony, the commander of the Engineering Battalion was absent and you were stepping in his place. Did you deliver any orders to the police during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not a single order did I give. But, here, if you look closely, you will see that it doesn't say the 5th Engineering Battalion. They talk about Obrenovic here. I don't know which Obrenovic that would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'm going to move on to another topic now. General Tolimir, at page 9508, lines 3 to 10, asked you the following question. He showed you -- sorry, he showed you some documents and then he asked: "Witness, on the basis of the documents that we've seen of the 13th, 14th, and 15th, that was dispatched to the Main Staff, does any of those documents contain any information about your unit, its activities or anything else other than the data about the wounding of two soldiers?" Now, I'd like to ask you about those two reports that were shown to you. You were shown one report from the 14th of July, going from the Drina Corps Command to the Main Staff, and a subsequent report that was sent from the Drina Corps Command to the Main Staff on the 15th of July. And on page 9502, lines 3, in answer -- after having read portions of the July 15th combat report of the Drina Corps, you answered that there was no information that was passed -- that was contained in that report about anything that was in your July 14th, 5th Battalion report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to P1604.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And under item 1, "The Enemy," paragraph 3, halfway through that paragraph, it says: "The remains of dispersed Muslim formations from the former Srebrenica enclave are moving towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje with the objective of crossing into Mount Udrc sector and on towards Tuzla and Zivinice." Is this not information that was contained in your 14th July 1995 report that there were Muslims who were coming from the Srebrenica enclave and had infiltrated the Konjevic Polje-Pobudje area?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when somebody speaks about Konjevic Polje, it's a pretty wide area. That's why I didn't consider that the Engineering Battalion was specifically mentioned. That's why.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not -- my question is not about whether the 5th Engineering Battalion was mentioned. I'm asking whether the information contained in your report, at -- which reads, for instance, a large enemy group infiltrated from the direction of Srebrenica into the region of Pobudje-Konjevic Polje, is that not reflected in this statement here in the Drina Corps Command report? Are we not talking about the same region, the Konjevic Polje region?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to emphasise one thing. We did not have an intelligence organ. So this could have been taken from somebody else's report. From a report made by some other infantry unit. Infantry units have things like that and it is quite possible that they have given this information to the higher command. Here it doesn't specifically say that they took it from our report. That's why I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Because the witness is here in the process -- the Prosecutor is here in the process of trying to connect this witness with lots of other things, I think that maybe the Prosecutor should specifically mention and show the documents that were yesterday shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a good proposal but we have a problem. We can't put both documents on the screen at the same time. You should figure out how to deal with this problem to connect the two documents, Ms. Hasan. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you say, sir, that the information contained in this Drina Corps Command report to the Main Staff is consistent with what is contained in your July 14th, 1995, report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't discuss a document which I didn't draft and did not take part in drafting it. That's why I don't know what is he talking about here in this document. I don't know whether he took it from Konjevic Polje. I don't know whether it is actually the same information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you any question that's any different from what General Tolimir asked you yesterday when he took you through this document. I'm simply asking you to respond to the same question, which is: I'm showing you information in this document and asking you whether that information reflects what was in your 14th July report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of this same report, 2 of the English version, and it's still page 1 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask for this document to be shown to the witness. And then we should see the exact words from this document which were then part of the report from the Drina Corps, because she is now telling him that some of his info has entered the report of the Drina Corps. But if we simply look at the route taken by the Muslims, well, that's really nothing special. Everybody knew where the Muslims were going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I can give the reference to -- I quoted exactly from the report itself, the 14th of July 5th Engineering Battalion report, where it says -- I can read it out again. Item 1, we looked at this yesterday: "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje." And then on page 3 of the English version, under item 4, which deals with the situation on the territory, it states: "A large enemy group infiltrated from the direction of Srebrenica into the region of Pobudje-Konjevic Polje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, it's quite time-consuming the way you are dealing with the documents again. We will soon have completed one hour of our today's hearing, and I think we have all these documents as documents admitted into evidence. Everybody, the parties, as the Chamber can draw conclusions from them. Everybody can compare the text. We have the witness -- the answers of the witness. You should try to complete your re-examination quite soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that was sent from Drina Corps to the Main Staff only contains the location or the direction of the movement of the Muslim forces. It doesn't mention the fact that they have stopped somewhere or that they have engaged in some activities. And also I didn't see any mention of Pobudje. So I don't think that that should be quoted as a reference. Because, what, somebody says the Tribunal so everything can be connected to the Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Many people do that. But, in fact, we shouldn't continue in this way. We have the documents, and it is up to the Chamber at the end of the day to -- to give weight to that and to compare the original text. My question for the Prosecution is to look at the clock and to see -- to hurry up with your re-examination and to conclude it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wanted to go through these documents that General Tolimir went through yesterday and he had skipped over certain parts that referred to information that is -- that is -- comes from or is identical to or consistent with the information that is contained in the 5th Engineering Battalion 14th July 1995 report. And if that exercise of comparison can be done, then I can conclude my re-examination at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This exercise can be done, if you want to have an interpretation by the witness. The -- the text of the two documents are in evidence. This is not the problem. If you want to have a comment by the witness, then put a question to the witness. In a way he can really answer it, but you -- I think we quite -- we can anticipate the position of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I think that I can conclude my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Sir, this concludes your testimony here in the courtroom. Thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to assist us. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the Court Usher will assist you leaving the courtroom. Thank you very much again. And first we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. McCloskey. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he is, and just one second before we get to that witness, if I could just request one thing of General Tolimir, since I don't really get a chance to see him and Mr. Gajic, that if there -- and to the Court that if there are issues, significant issues related to CLSS official translations, as there was in the last cross-examination and examination, that those issues be brought up to the Court outside the presence of the witness and well in advance so that we can all deal with them. Clearly the explanations that were given in front of the witness may have affected the witness's evaluation of the document himself. We didn't object in that situation. There was no harm done at all because all of these issues related to this document and the words and the translation had been fully discussed in the previous trial so it was nothing new to him. But I'm just asking the General and Mr. Gajic that if they do have significant issues with the CLSS official translation, let us know and we'll try to sort them out and allow the Court to see those as well. But, really, I would prefer it not be done in front of the witness like that. The second point I don't want to forget is this next witness is -- he is fully open and all, but he will need a caution. I would request a caution. He is the commander of the Zvornik Brigade Rocevic area battalion. I believe it's the 2nd Battalion. And also something I discussed briefly with Mr. Gajic is, you will hear from this witness and from my summary that his memory about exact dates was not good and that he knows that the first time he learned of prisoners at the Rocevic school was a few days after the fall of Srebrenica but he doesn't remember the exact date. And I just wanted to offer that it's the Prosecution's position that that date that he first was made aware that there were prisoners at the Rocevic school is 14 July. I don't know if they want to agree with me on that, but there's voluminous evidence and indications of that. But that's so that it helps make more sense out of the chronology when -- because he doesn't remember it himself. We believe it's the 14th of July that will be the -- fundamentally the beginning of his chronology. My summary of this witness is a little bit longer than I prefer but my questioning will be shorter than I prefer -- or not that I prefer but that I -- shorter than what is needed and I think we should get everything done relatively quickly so that we can get on to Mr. Brunborg, hopefully start him today, if we're lucky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are very optimistic. And, of course, this is affected also by the length of the summary. I hope it is really a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, when you look at the length and the detail and the cross-examination of these witnesses, these are very summary in nature, though I try to give you the most specific facts as I can so that you and anybody that is looking at this testimony will be able to make as much sense as they can out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom and the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, and thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to give you a caution. You know, in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, there we have Rule 90(E) which I would like to read out for you. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Did you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey has questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And first can you state your name for the record slowly so that we can get it down.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Srecko Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you testify in this courtroom in the case of the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. This, as I'm sure you recall me telling you, will be a little different. We will try to make this a little shorter for you and us, so I'll ask you a couple of questions. Have you had a chance to listen to your Popovic testimony in the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell me that there was one addition or clarification that you wanted to make the Court aware of today?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So aside from this addition or clarification that we'll get to in a minute, if you were asked the same questions today as you were in the Popovic case, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that event --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see the General's hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, it's not clear to me if the answers would be the same, then does the addition include these topics or does the addition contain some other topics? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the same topic as always and I think it's an addition and clarification as he stated. And he will soon tell us that, and that will be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So given that basic record, I would like now to offer, and all I have is 65 ter numbers this time, Mr. President, the transcript of his testimony in Popovic which is 0663, and 0664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents will be received, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 06663 shall be assigned Exhibit P1772, admitted under seal. And 65 ter document 6664 shall be assigned exhibit number P1773. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then associated exhibits admitted through this witness would be a "Drinski" magazine article, 06077, and a Zvornik Brigade transportation record, 00283. I'd offer those and I'll wait for the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you sure that the last number is correct in your list? This is 65 ter 03440.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Our number is 00283 but we'll, of course -- I'm getting confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's an older version of the sheet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. And I have heard that this is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 00283 was assigned exhibit number P1596 as part of the 92 bis Prosecution witnesses' associated documents pursuant to the Trial Chamber's public oral decision dated 31st January 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The "Drinski" magazine article will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the other exhibit on that list is already in evidence and we don't wish any others to come in, so that should do it for the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We would like to receive the number of 65 ter 06077.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The mentioned document shall be assigned Exhibit P1774. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Acimovic, I have a summary of a -- of your testimony. It won't contain everything in it, but I think if I can read that summary first, then you can offer your addition and the summary may help make your addition put it in context, all right? Srecko Acimovic was born in the village of Rocevic in the Zvornik municipality in May 1967. In July of 1995, Mr. Acimovic was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade and held the rank of reserve lieutenant. Mr. Acimovic did not recall the exact date but testified that in the days following the fall of Srebrenica, he learned from locals from the village of Rocevic that Muslim prisoners were being killed in front of the elementary school in Rocevic and that a local Serb woman had been injured during the killings. Sometime between 8.00 and 9.00 p.m. that day, Mr. Acimovic, together with the local priest and the president of the local commune went to the Rocevic school and noticed soldiers there who appeared to be under the influence of alcohol. Mr. Acimovic testified he did not see the prisoners but heard people shouting from the school gym, pleading for water and permission to use the bathroom. Acimovic asked the soldiers where the prisoners had come from and who had brought them to the school, but the soldiers did not answer his questions and denied him permission to talk to their commanding officer. After about half an hour, Mr. Acimovic left the school and went towards the battalion command in the village of Malesici. On his way, he stopped at Kozluk and called the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade located in the Standard factory near Zvornik. He asked about the prisoners that were being held in the Rocevic school. The duty officer told Mr. Acimovic that he had no knowledge of the situation, and Acimovic asked to be connected to the Zvornik Brigade commander, or to Dragan Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. The duty officer told Mr. Acimovic that neither of them was present at the time. Vujadin Popovic, the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the Drina Corps, arrived at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters while Acimovic was still on the telephone with the duty officer and was put on the phone. Mr. Acimovic spoke to Popovic and explained that soldiers were killing prisoners in front of the school located in the centre of Rocevic. Popovic told Acimovic that the prisoners would be exchanged the following morning. After his conversation with Popovic, Acimovic returned to Rocevic to convey the information he had just learned about the exchange of the prisoners to the local priest and the president of the local commune. Acimovic spoke to the president of the local commune and together with him went back to the school. At the school, Acimovic testified that he tried to persuade the soldiers to provide water to the prisoners and to give them access to a toilet. Acimovic testified that the soldiers eventually agreed to this. After this second visit to the school, Mr. Acimovic left and returned to his battalion command where he informed Vujo Lazarevic, the assistant battalion commander for morale, legal and religious affairs, and Mitar Lazarevic, the desk officer for general affairs at the battalion command, about the situation in Rocevic. Between 1.00 and 2.00 a.m. the next day, while still at the battalion command, Mr. Acimovic received a coded telegram, ordering the detachment of a platoon of soldiers to be used for the execution of the prisoners at the Rocevic school. Mr. Acimovic testified that he decided not to detach any of their personnel for that purpose and sent a response to that effect. Mr. Acimovic testified that he could not recollect who the signatory of the order was, but that his response was sent to either the duty officer or the assistant for security and intelligence of the Zvornik Brigade. Forty-five minutes to an hour later, Mr. Acimovic received another telegram that once again ordered the detachment of personnel to carry out the execution of the prisoners and stated that Acimovic was to inform his company commanders and the battalion command of the order. Mr. Acimovic consulted with his assistants, Vujo Lazarevic and Mitar Lazarevic -- excuse me, he consulted with his assistants. Mr. Acimovic testified that they reaffirmed their agreement not to obey the order and again sent a response setting out their refusal to dispatch personnel to carry out the execution of the prisoners. Thereafter, Mr. Acimovic contacted the company commanders to determine whether they had received the telegram and to inform them of their response to the order. Mr. Acimovic received confirmation that Mr. Stjepanovic, commander of the 1st Infantry Company, and two other company commanders had received, possibly through their deputies, the subject telegram. Ten minutes after receiving the second telegram, at approximately 2.30 a.m., Drago Nikolic, who Mr. Acimovic described as the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the Zvornik Brigade, contacted Mr. Acimovic by phone at the battalion command. Nikolic told Acimovic that the order had come from above and had to be followed. Acimovic testified that he explained to Nikolic that they did not have enough people to allocate to this task and that they would not be carrying out the order. As the conversation drew to a close, Nikolic gave Acimovic until 7.00 a.m. to carry out the order. At around 7.00 or 8.00 a.m. that day, Nikolic called Acimovic to check whether he had complied with the order. Acimovic testified that he once again told Nikolic that they would not follow the order. In response, Nikolic told Acimovic that if he did not gather the men as ordered, that he - meaning Acimovic - would personally have to engage in the task with his people. Nikolic told Acimovic to meet him in Rocevic at 9.00 or 10.00 a.m. After speaking to Drago Nikolic, Acimovic called the brigade duty officer and told him of the prisoners at the school and asked for the Chief of Staff of the brigade to call him back. Shortly after that, Acimovic drove to the school in Rocevic to meet Nikolic. However, Nikolic wasn't there. While at the school, Acimovic saw many more unknown people and soldiers in the school-yard and at least a dozen corpses lying on the grass in front of the school bathroom. Mr. Acimovic then encountered Vujadin Popovic at the school, whom he had spoken to over the telephone the day before. Popovic yelled at Acimovic for not having brought men with him pursuant to the order. After threatening and pressuring Acimovic to comply, Popovic instructed Acimovic to see whether there was anybody in the school-yard who was willing to take part in the executions. Acimovic testified he refused to do so. Acimovic then left Popovic and did not follow his order. Acimovic testified that he returned a short time later and suggested to Popovic that the prisoners should be returned to where they'd come from or evacuated to the barracks in Kozluk. Popovic then called the brigade duty officer and requested that they urgently send vehicles and trucks to Rocevic. Approximately 30 to 40 minutes later, one truck arrived in the school-yard. Popovic told Acimovic he needed more trucks, but Acimovic testified he refused to help Popovic with this task. While present at the school with Popovic, Acimovic heard Popovic tell one of the soldiers that all the prisoners were to be killed somewhere nearby the school. Sometime between 11.30 and 12.15, Acimovic returned to the 2nd Battalion headquarters. Dragan Jovic, Veljko Ivanovic and Djordje Nikolic, all members of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, stayed behind at the Rocevic school. When he arrived at the 2nd Battalion headquarters, Acimovic informed Mitar Lazarevic and Vujo Lazarevic about what had happened and attempted to establish contact with Dragan Obrenovic. He did not manage to reach him but briefed the Zvornik Brigade duty officer on what was happening at the Rocevic school. At some later stage, Obrenovic told Acimovic that he was in the field at the time and was not aware of the events happening at Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Acimovic, in that context of the summary, can you tell us what it is you wanted to add and why it is you wanted to add it to this testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say just one detail which has to do with my departure from the school-yard. During my first testimony here before the ICTY, I said that I passed by these three drivers and did not stay there or talk to them. However, after the testimony of these same witnesses here at ICTY, specifically I mean one of these drivers, who said that as I was leaving the school in Rocevic, I told them that I couldn't watch that with my own eyes and that they had to drive the prisoners, that reminded me what I actually did say on this occasion and I feel that it is my duty to tell that to the Trial Chamber. As I was going by these drivers, I said, Let me just warn you that our unit has nothing to do with this. I shall not take part in all this, nor can I watch this with my own eyes. I'm leaving and I'm going to Malesici. And one of these drivers, who testified here, said, Sreco, what am I going to do? I have to do it because I was sent from the brigade. Once again, I drew their attention to this. I said, Just let it be clear that I warned you and I'm going to leave now. So I left for Malesici. This is the detail which I felt the need to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session just for a second out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I've just one question. Today's transcript during your reading of the summary, page 29, lines 8, 9, and 10, I'm not sure if you were recorded correctly. I see here: "Mr. Acimovic consulted with his assistants, Vujo Lazarevic and Mitar Lazarevic." And then you said, which is not recorded, "Excuse me." I don't know what -- if it refers to this sentence, because then you continued: "He consulted with his assistants." Is that correctly recorded or was there something different, what you read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's correct and I -- the summary was meant to mean that his assistants were the two Lazarevics. And I -- just let me check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that correct, are those -- the Lazarevics your assistants?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just ask a couple of questions to clarify some things. You've mentioned that you heard that a local Serb woman was injured outside this school that day. Can you tell us what is your understanding -- you know, what kind of injury she suffered, from who or from what source?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what the president of the local commune and the priest informed me about. It was the president of the local commune of Rocevic. And it was close to my family house. They told me that the local woman sustained an entry and exit wound and that she was hit by a bullet from an infantry weapon, that this was done by the soldiers who had brought the prisoners and who, while killing the prisoners, shot in the direction of the place where the local woman was, and as a result, she sustained the entry and exit wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever confirm that that actually happened as it was described to you, to that woman?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't check that, but it's definitely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified at length about receiving what you've described as a telegram, and I believe "telegram" is the same in Serbian as it is in English, a telegram, a coded telegram ordering you to form an execution squad to kill the prisoners. Telegrams can be different in different places. So could you explain to us what a telegram is in the context that you meant, how it was transmitted, how it was received and all that, so we can get an idea of what you mean when you say your battalion received a telegram.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, and at that specific time, I was sleeping. My assistants, whom we already mentioned, woke me up. One of them woke me up and told me to get down to the battalion command and to be informed as we had received a telegram, that they should tell me what this was all about. When I came down, they told me that the telegram was encrypted and that they had decoded it. I then read it and it ordered the command of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, that is to say, myself, to provide one platoon of soldiers for the execution of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard about various means of communications available; the PTT telephone, the induction telephone, the RUP radios, the teletype communications. What kind of communication did the telegram come over?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Over an induction telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when the -- your soldier or communications person or whoever picks up the phone, what kind of information does he get that is this telegram? Does he get a series of numbers, does he get -- words, does he get Morse code? What is he actually hearing that is the telegram?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the kind of telegram. If the telegram is encrypted, then the communications officer notes down the codes. When he notes down the entire contents of the telegram that means all the codes which have been forwarded, he then calls the duty officer at the battalion command and in the same manner, over the phone, he forwards the contents of the telegram which he also notes into the notebook which contains the telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm almost done. I see it's time to break. Let me just almost finish this topic. So when this officer answering the phone gets the verbal code and writes down those verbal codes, what are those verbal codes usually? You know, what kind of numbers or letters are they or -- just for our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Probably letters, numbers, alternately some expressions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is it fair to conclude that a person with a code book that can decipher those coded numbers or letters takes the code book and can decode the telegram to figure out what it actually says in Serbian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, a telegram cannot be decoded without a table which every battalion command had for certain specific times of day, and it was usually something that the battalion command had. So when it was that sort of telegram you would take the table for decoding a telegram and then, in accordance with the table, the very same telegram would be decoded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have someone special in your battalion that did that or could anybody do it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, every signalman is trained to decode various kinds of telegrams, and I believe that every member of the battalion command should have known how to use the table, though there is suspicion that these people were not always able to do that or capable of doing it, because these were privates who were deployed to command duties within the battalion command. Possibly they may have needed help or not. It all depended on the particular person and the particular moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Last question. Do you recall who deciphered the telegrams that night that we're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these were the persons we have already mentioned, namely, Vujo Lazarevic and Mitar Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Acimovic, go to that -- sort of that second day that you've spoke of briefly, where you had just said a few things to your drivers that you clarified for us and then you left the school. Was it that day that -- that the prisoners at the Rocevic school were eventually transported away, or did they stay at the school longer?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that day they were transported, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where -- what -- where were they transported, if you -- if you learned?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: As you learned in the course of these proceedings, it was a location in Kozluk where they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now let me go back to that first day, where you have said that this -- you first became aware of the prisoners at the school about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. Then you eventually said that you've gone to Kozluk and that's where you called the brigade, a duty officer, and you said they put Popovic on the phone. Do you remember roughly what time of day it was that they put Popovic on the phone? Was it still light out? Was it dark? Just your best recollection of, you know, when that was.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was dark, definitely, but the only thing is I wasn't looking for Popovic. I asked -- when I was asking to speak with the commander or the Chief of Staff, when they told me that they weren't there, what I said was, Were any other members of the command, of the Zvornik Brigade, available. And I was told that none of them were present, and that was when I asked, Is anyone there that I could speak about this matter with? And then the duty operations officer said that Vujadin Popovic was there from the Drina Corps. The security chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So it was -- it was -- was it dark when they put Popovic on the line?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm not 100 per cent sure. I cannot assert that 100 per cent. I cannot say that it was dark. It was summer, so it gets dark a bit later. So it was possible, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what time it gets dark in Bosnia in -- you know, in July?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: From 9.00 to 9.30, that would be the time. 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so if you were correct when you say you were first alerted to the prisoners in the school at 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., roughly how much later did you make your way to Kozluk to -- and end up talking to Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. When I found out about the situation at Rocevic, I spent maybe some 15 minutes there and then I needed another 15 minutes to get to Kozluk, so this is 30 minutes. And then the conversation itself, perhaps lasted for about 15 minutes, and that would be my approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So that -- I'll just call it the first evening when -- when Popovic told you that the Muslim prisoners at the Rocevic school would be exchanged the next day, had you heard any reports of Muslim prisoners being killed in the 4th Battalion area around Orahovac or anywhere else, most of the day that day, beginning in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any information at all about any prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility. And up until that time, I didn't know about it in Rocevic either, until I saw it with my own eyes. Any kind of information or report from the brigade or any other kind of information was really not available to me. I did not have any access to any kind of information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would end at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Tolimir, now you may commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I would wish for peace in this house and for these proceedings and my cross-examination of this witness may end according to God's will and not according to mine. I would like to welcome the witness, wish him a pleasant stay here and I would also like to him to have a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir, for coming. I would like you to respond to certain questions according to your best recollection. If you find that I am stating something erroneously, please feel free to correct me or to mention if something does not comport with the way you remember it. I have one more thing to ask you. When I put my question to you I'm going to say "thank you" after I complete putting my question to you. You can monitor the screen in front of you. When the letters stop moving, then you can begin answering, because that will give the interpreters enough time to translate everything that I'm saying and that you are saying, because everything has to be entered correctly into the transcript. And I'm thanking you in advance for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the beginning of the transcript for today, on page 1, when we were dealing with the summary, Mr. McCloskey said -- he actually asked you when you found out that Muslim civilians were being killed in Rocevic. My question is this -- this was on page 25, actually, when the summary was read. I am going to identify the passage. He said, Are you aware that Muslim civilians were being killed? So my question is: He said the Muslim population, I apologise, I have to be precise. He asked about the Muslim population, when you found out that the Muslim population was being killed in Rocevic. So my question is: Sir, did you find out that the Muslim population in Rocevic was being killed or were they Muslim prisoners that were being killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see those Muslim prisoners in order to be able to tell for yourself whether these people were citizens or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't close to the location. When I came to the school, this is some 40 metres away from there, so I wasn't able to definitely see whether those people had any kind of military insignia or whether they were just wearing civilian clothing. It was summer. So I really couldn't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the question was long and I would like to repeat it in a different format. And that is: Did you see any Muslim prisoners in Rocevic at all? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any of them, but I did hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. McCloskey was reading the summary, amongst other things, it said there that you said to Popovic that prisoners were being killed in Rocevic. Did you hear that when the summary was being read out by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether you told Popovic that prisoners in Rocevic were being killed when you spoke with him on the telephone and did you ask him why those prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what did you ask him? Can you please tell us for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before I said anything else, I informed him about the situation in Rocevic. He told me that those same prisoners were going to be exchanged the following day and that I shouldn't be too dramatic about this whole matter because that wasn't my job. I also drew his attention, and I think I talked to him with a raised voice. I asked him, Are you normal? Something to the effect that they were guarding those people, they were killing them in the school-yard, that they were wounding the nearby civilians and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You told him that prisoners were getting killed in the school-yard and you told him that one woman was killed -- was wounded. Exactly what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I told him both of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 02064 in e-court, please. This is a transcript of the conversation of the investigators with this witness in Banja Luka in 2001 and 2002, so that we could help the witness to follow what we're going to be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. 02064, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question was simply if that is a 65 ter number and not a P or D number. But I think now we can take it that's it a 65 ter number. And one remark for the record, you were referring first to page 1 of today's transcript. This is, of course, an error. And then you were referring to page 25, but the summary read into the transcript starts with page 26, line 24. There should be another reference. I couldn't find that specific portion when you were referring to Muslim population instead of prisoners. But that was just a remark for the record. You should continue and question the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 25, the witness answers and he provides his particulars, his first and last name, his place and date of birth, and then after that, he is asked by Mr. McCloskey if he had information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about the Muslim population being killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there is no need -- thank you very much, but there's no need to discuss it. I just wanted to have it on the record. The summary started on page 26 and not page 25. At a later stage some people would like to find out where it is, and that was just a correction. Please continue your questioning. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could it be clear, I never said "population," so maybe that's an error, but I think it's an important thing to clarify. I've always said "prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't find the word "population" myself, when I was looking for that word which you put to the witness. If you could give us a reference, that would be fine; otherwise, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and I also thank Mr. McCloskey. This is how it was interpreted to me and this is how I wrote it down. Since I take notes, it is possible that I made a mistake, and I thank Mr. McCloskey for correcting it for the record, that he was speaking about prisoners. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the transcript now. We're looking at the page ... I can't see the page number on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll up just so that I can look at the page. But I can see actually in the English version that it is page 1. Can we now look at page 8? Thank you. Page 8 in the Serbian and that is on lines 7, 8, and 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now you can see line 6, where it says: "Yes, is coordinating and according to the situation commands in the event that the commander is away or in order to carry out orders pursuant to orders in a specific time-period." And then it goes on to line 9, if I understood you correctly, the Chief of Staff coordinates the security organ and so on. And you answer, yes. In order to be clear --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is something wrong with the translation. Something is not quite right and this is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. That's what I thought. There was something wrong with the order. So the security organ who was -- who were they subordinated to in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: To the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now let us look at the rule, what it says about that. And then I'm going to put questions to you about that. All right. Now we're going to look at D148. You were explaining it here, and then the translation was wrong so now it's important for us to look at the actual rule. We're looking at the rule on the screen right now. This is the brigade rules about -- for infantry, motorised, mountain, alpine, marine and light brigades. This is the rules by the Army of Republika Srpska. Are you aware that these rules were being applied in your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I never had the opportunity to acquaint myself with this particular rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We are now going to look at what the brigade command does. In the Serbian, this is page 64, and in the English it's page 37. Can you please look at Article 115, which states, I will read: "The brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units. He bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade command and subordinate commands for the state of morale, for security, and combat readiness, for training and for the proper performance of tasks. The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their execution and demands their strict execution, regardless of difficulties that arise." My question is: These powers that are referred to in the rule, is that something that your brigade commander enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then did he transfer these powers to his deputy or to the chief?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what it says here, about the duties of the brigade commander, does that also apply to the battalion, in terms of the battalion composition?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there anything different that would be different from what we have just read?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: There are similarities. I think that's more or less that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at what the security organ does. This is page 66 in the Serbian, and page 38 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And let us compare with what you said. I don't want to be reading the ten pages of the report where you were explaining to the investigators who does what. All right. Now we're going to look at Article 122, which refers to the security organ, we're seeing it. Thank you, e-court. "The security organ is a specialised organ of the command which organises and implements measures and procedures of counter-intelligence support. It also participates in recommending, organising and implementing security and self-protection measures which concern the command and other subjects of self-protection." Second paragraph: "In terms of expertise, it directs the work of the intelligence and security organs of subordinate units. It organises and directs their work, provides assistance and controls their activities in completing counter-intelligence activities and duties." And so on and so forth. Then it goes on to speak about the cooperation with the brigade forces. My question to you is: Is the bearer of all measures and activities implemented by the security organ the brigade commander or is it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the security organ implement measures and organise things for which the main responsibility is borne by the commander and other subjects of self-protection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let us now look at what they do, because we're going to come to that. At one place you were asked what were the powers of the security organ and you told the investigators that that includes work with prisoners of war. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember saying it, but if you say that I said it, then I probably did say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm just going to read out some other regulations and then we're going to discuss the practice that was in force in your brigade. I'm kindly asking you now to look at paragraph -- this is on page 125 in the Serbian, 79 in the English, and this is logistics for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is paragraph 295 that we can see on our screen. In the English, this is the last one on the page, and in the Serbian it is the one-but-last.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 295, I quote: "Logistics support for prisoners of war includes the provision of necessary supplies and health care. Provisions of supplies to prisoners in prisoner stations and other locations while they are under the jurisdiction of the armed forces is organised by logistics and other organs in units which have captured them. The escort for prisoners of war in camps is organised and implemented by the Territorial Defence Staffs, in collaboration with socio-political communities." Based on what I have just read, my question is: Did you, in the brigade or in the battalion, have any forces that could provide logistic support for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. And if you permit me, I would like to say something else. You are reading certain rules of the former JNA which refer to the Territorial Defence. I never had the chance to become familiar with these rule-books. You probably know, you have been informed about specifically how I was appointed to my duties. So, pursuant to that, I would like to inform you one more time that even though I have already been asked about certain rules, if you wish, I could make things easier for you. There's a possibility that I made a mistake somewhere. It was something that I never studied. What I said, I spoke on the basis of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm merely trying to recall, for the purposes of the record, who had what obligation and duty, and I wanted you to tell us how things looked like in your unit based on your recollections. Now I'm going to ask you a question. Did you have a security organ in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he have anybody else working with him in that organ or any other soldiers subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he able, on his own, to escort, interrogate, and feed any prisoners that could have been captured by the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the same situation also in the brigade command? Did the organ for security there had any subordinated soldiers or any ability to take care or feed the prisoners? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
