utterances.text: That's a different story. I think that a unit such as a brigade should have manpower available for that purpose. I mean, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So a brigade can have it but not an organ of the brigade such as a security or some other organ of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that you're talking here about all the soldiers subordinated to the brigade commander, just like the organ for security is subordinated?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move now to page 14, if I'm not mistaken -- no, page 10 of your statement, which is 65 ter 02064. I would like to go back to that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at page 10 and further on, where you talk about the duty operative officer. I would like to pose several questions in relation to your previous answer. And I'm definitely going to give you a reference, in case that you're unable to remember what exactly you said. It is not my goal to tell you what my answers would have been. Maybe I would have given the same answers. My goal here is to establish what was supposed to be done. Thank you. Was there a duty operative officer in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your brigade commander command over his subordinate units through his duty operative or directly?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: That would depend on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain this situation then?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably the brigade commander, when he has no possibility to directly communicate his orders, then he would do it through his duty operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would such a situation occur when the brigade commander is absent? For instance, he is in the field without any means of communication so he cannot communicate to a battalion commander or somebody else who is subordinated to him in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the situation in the field. It all depends from case to case. It means that there is a number of different options depending on the situation in the field and depending on the task at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is as follows: Is the duty operative in the position to command the brigade if the commander and the Chief of Staff are within the zone of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, something like that never happened. It would mostly be the Chief of Staff or the commander who would almost always be accessible. Now I cannot claim that something like that never happened but I don't know of such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question, based on this answer, is as a follows: Is the duty operative able, in any case, to command the brigade if both the Chief of Staff and the brigade commander are inside the zone of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there are some military rules which say that in the absence of the brigade commander and the Chief of Staff, and in case that no communication with them can be established, that in such a case if an order should be issued, it would be the duty operative who would issue such an order. But I think that it never happened that the duty operative would issue some sort of a more serious order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to your battalion and make an analogy. Was it possible in your battalion that any officer in the battalion could command the battalion without your approval?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It would all depend on the situation in the field, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So, when leaving the zone of responsibility of the battalion, does that mean that the battalion commander has the duty to tell exactly who is going to replace him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the same true for the brigade and the corps and other units, that there should always be a person designated by the commander who is going to replace the commander if he is absent?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the reason for that the fact that some less experienced officer, like staff-sergeant, for instance, could be filling the place of the duty operative and that is why there is a need for the commander to designate the person who is going to replace him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Does that mean that the duty operative, in your unit and in all other units, would only transmit the orders issued by commanders and Chiefs of Staffs to their subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is how it was. That is my opinion. Now whether that's correct, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to carry on the analogy, does that mean that the duty operative can be held responsible for the situation in the brigade regardless of whether the commander and the Chief of Staff are present or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: This question demands a slightly deeper analysis. It all depends on the situation. Does this duty operative have already some task assigned to him or not? I think that this is a rather complex question, more complex than I can give you my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to clarify it now. Was the duty operative, under any circumstances, in a position to command over your battalion and to be held responsible for the activities of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: There were situations when the duty operative would issue certain orders. I cannot claim now that he would issue those orders in his own name or whether he merely transmitted those orders. It all depends on the situation, you know. I can't really give you a detailed answer and a detailed analysis of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now let us take a look at your battalion. Was the duty operative in your battalion in a position to command over the battalion or a smaller unit in your absence?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I wish to emphasise that most probably he would not take it upon himself to issue any more serious order, if he is in a position to get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if he, by chance, assigns a task to somebody, does that mean that he has the duty to inform you that he had issued such a task while you were absent?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So the duty organs in the battalion, in the brigade, can we say that their main task is to regulate the situation in accordance with the rules of service in relation to everyday tasks and that commanding is not within their purview?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I told that you it all depends on the situation and that you can't apply the same rules every time. In most cases, the duty operative -- or, rather, in the battalion there was no duty operative, there was just a duty officer, duty officer of the battalion. So it all depended on the situation but he would mainly coordinate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell us what is this coordination all about?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I again have to emphasise that it depends on the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if the duty officer in the battalion or in the brigade is unclear about something, does he have the right to apply to the duty operative in a higher unit? Meaning the one from the battalion to the brigade, the one from the brigade to the corps?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a rule -- is there a duty defined in the rules, his duty that he had to consult with others in case he was unclear about what to do?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would not exclude the possibility of such a coordination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown page 17 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading the first, second, third, fourth line. Thank you. This is page 18 in English. The investigator asked you - we can see that - on line 2: "Is there some specific unit within the brigade that would be in charge of taking over these prisoners?" And then you say: "I think that that is the duty of the security organ." And then you go on to say, on line 5 -- well, the investigator tells you: "And then that would take them back." And then you say: "Yes. In any case that is true." And then in line 8, you say, and who, then, would they report -- who would they report this incident to in the brigade? One of the two, it depends which one is at the present at the moment. And then you told the investigator, in response to his question, you said the security organs would take the prisoners. Would they physically turn up at your battalion to take the prisoners? And you say, in line 12: "I mentioned earlier that I didn't have such experience. All of this now that we are talking about, it's all just assumptions." So my question is: The commanders, the komandirs, the soldiers, if they learned about the prisoners, would the security organs learn about them as well? Who can find out about these matters?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on which unit we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. But in any case, who would be the first person to be informed about a capture? Would it be the person who actually captured him or somebody working in a command?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about here about the coordination between a soldier, komandir and commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So does that mean that they have to inform their superiors about the fact that they captured somebody in the zone of their combat activity?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then you, as the commander of the battalion, you would call up the security organ and assign him a task in relation to those captured people.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I could not issue order to security organs. They had their duties and could not take such orders, but I informed the duty operative about it. It means that I tried to inform the brigade organs about such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise for asking you, because you did not have such a specific example in your practice and I certainly wish to emphasise that. Now, since you did not have any such example in your practice, as you stated here in this statement, page 18, does that mean that the brigade would be informed about the prisoners from their subordinated units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about individual cases. Individual cases, then, yes, probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a security organ in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, could it be made clear if we're talking about the prisoners that are the subject of his testimony or if this is just hypothetical, because the prisoners of the testimony are a very unique situation and it is impossible to tell from the question whether we're talking about the prisoners at Rocevic school or capturing a prisoner on the front line. If that could be made clear, it might help us with the meaning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I, myself, was wondering where these kind of questions would lead us. Perhaps you can explain that or go ahead with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. The witness and I are talking about the situation as it existed in the field. Later on, we are going to talk about specific topics when it is time to talk about specific topics. Right now he was talking about jurisdictions, and I simply want to ask him whether a security organ would receive an order from the commander who -- to deal with the prisoners who were captured within the zone of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I want to ask him whether he had a security organ in the battalion and whether he would assign him tasks in relation to prisoners who appeared within his zone.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I really want your questions to be direct and more specific so that they would be more clear to me. A moment ago, when speaking about prisoners, you were saying something, but I have to say they were not my prisoners. They were not captured by my prisoners. They were not brought there by my --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They were not captured by my soldiers and they were not brought by my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I thought that you were asking about me about rules in general and not specifically, about specific prisoners in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, exactly, I was asking you about rules. You said that there were no prisoners within your zone.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Within my defence zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Within your defence zone. And they were not captured by your soldiers. They were brought there by some unknown soldiers. So that is why I was asking you, so far, only about the rules and general situation. I apologise for not clarifying this sufficiently. My following question is as follows: If the organs of the military police are engaged, on the orders of their superior, on tasks of securing war prisoners which appeared within the zone, such as the case in Rocevici, who would then be in the position to issue them orders about this, or, rather, who -- from whom would they receive their orders to perform such a task?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Military police. From whom does the military police receive the task to engage their forces in support of war prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question. As I told you, it all depends on the situation. It depends on who specifically was then in a situation to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To whom is the military police unit within the brigade subordinated? To whom are subordinated all the military policemen in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all units within the brigade are normally subordinated to the commander. However, the military police company would coordinate it, first of all, with the security organs. They had some sort of a close relationship with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it means that they had a certain relationship with the security organs in addition to their duties and relations with the commander. So their relation with the security organs, was that something that was widely known within the brigade regulated by the rules?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not sure about this. I -- I really can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your practice, was it known to the commander, to the Chief of Staff, to everybody in the brigade, that the security organs and the military police have certain relations in -- with the approval of the commander, or did they do these things illegally, secretly?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, it would be with the approval of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, I apologise for this. When you arrived to the school at Rocevici, were you able to identify any person there who was providing security for the prisoners? I mean, did you know any person there and did you know to which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I already stated that earlier, in my earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true you said that on page 18. You said that you were informed by the president of the local community and by the local priest that there were some prisoners in the school in the village. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you on duty at the time when you were informed about this or were you outside of the unit, taking rest, or somewhere else for your personal needs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was taking a short break. That's how I would put it. I went to my family house to take care of some personal needs but just for a brief time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then, as a member of the brigade and an inhabitant of the Rocevici village, engage in order to resolve the situation which had arisen in a positive way, the situation that you were informed about by the president of the local commune and the priest so that you would help them and do something about their concern?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was not resolving any situation there but, as I told you, I did what I did. First of all, my duty was to inform the brigade command about the events that were taking place in Rocevici and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you fulfil your military duty by doing that, even though you were not on duty at the moment? I mean, informing the superior command about the events which were taking place in the brigade's zone of responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because this was an extraordinary event. I felt duty-bound to inform the brigade command about this, especially as such things were happening in Rocevici at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, being humane, did you also engage in order to improve the conditions for the prisoners, did you request that they be given food, water and so on, when you learned that they would be exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was engaged about that for a brief time for purely humane reasons, because I felt pity and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained that on page 23, in line 7, and for the sake of the transcript, I wanted to mention that. Thank you. Now if could you please have a look at page 26, because I will be asking you questions in connection with that. It's page 26. And specifically, lines 8 to 18. Let have a look at lines 17 and 18 about which I will ask you the first question, so that you can find your bearings. It's page 28 in the English version of the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, when did Mr. Popovic tell you that the prisoners who were at the school in Rocevici would be exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, when I had contact with him when I was informing the brigade about the events in Rocevici, that was when he told me, Don't panic too much, these people will be exchanged tomorrow. And on the basis of these words of his, I sensed a sort of relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my question: Were you aware that there were also soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska who were taken prisoners by the Army of BiH, and was it logical for you to accept such an explanation that they could be exchanged ones for the others?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: There was probably such a possibility. It was a matter of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible that such an exchange be postponed because of one or the other side which may have imposed certain conditions for the exchange so that it didn't take place?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot answer such questions because this was not the kind of information that I had at my disposal, and consequently, I think that I'm not the right person to answer such questions. I cannot give any kind of answer to questions of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I didn't find any mentioning of exchange of prisoners on that page we have in front of us. Can you help me, indicating which part of the -- this OTP interview you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said on page 26, in lines 8 to 18. Line 17, I quote. I quote line 17: "They said again that on the next day they would be evacuated and would be exchanged." I apologise, it's possible that I mentioned the wrong page number in English. It's page 27 in English and I probably said page 28. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said 26. And now, hopefully, we have the right page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is actually page 29 in English version, line 17. I was reading from what I have. Page 26, line 17. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now we are really confused. Which page is the right one? I have no idea. First you said 26; then 27; then 29; then, again, 26. Which is the correct page in English? I don't find the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's page 29 in the English version and page 26 in the Serbian language. Line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's wait if we will find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could I ask in the future that we're provided with not only the page in the English version but the line in the English version. That's just normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have page 30. It seems to be line 5, or 3 through 5 on page 30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President, 3 to 5 on page -- is it 30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have page 30 in English. But I don't know if we have the relevant page in B/C/S on the screen. We need your clear guidance for the Registry so that they can display the right pages, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have read it out for the transcript. It's page 26, line 17, in the Serbian language, and it's part of the 65 ter 02264, which I received from the Prosecution. And my legal assistant says that these are lines 4 and 5 on page 29 in the English version. That is to say, page 30 -- I'm sorry, because I don't speak or read English -- thank you. These are lines 30 in the English language. It means 26 in -- what are the lines, Aleksandar?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 3 to 5 on page 30, as requested by Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now on the screen. After all this confusion, we found the relevant part. Now put a question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question for the witness before this confusion arose as my mistake, as I can't speak English, was this: When were you told that the persons who were prisoners and held in Rocevici would be exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: After that, when I first contacted the duty operations officer that is to say, when I called the brigade to report to them about the events that I told you about and that were taking place in Rocevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall now move to another part of 65 ter 02063, your statement, where you discuss the problems of the so-called encrypted telegram. That's the subject. And it's page 7 of the second section of the statement. The date is the 17th of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see in e-court page 7 about which I will be asking questions, so that the witness could see what I'm asking him in connection with the telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line in B/C/S and which page in English and line in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 7 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 1, 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line and page in English? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a suggestion. There's an old rule that statements like this are really not relevant unless they're used to either refresh someone's recollection or impeach them. This witness recollects about these situations. He can answer questions all about it. This going through his statements that's neither impeaching him nor giving him any recollection is -- seems to be a waste of time, especially since we can't find the English version. So perhaps if we went back to some traditional rules and just asked the witness about the topic, which I'm not even sure are in contest, we could save some time. Because I think we have now -- there's a couple of interviews that this gentleman gave, and I think we have 02063 is not the interview we've been talking about, which was September of 2010. This is another one, I think in March. So -- or we could take an early break and have Mr. Gajic really get together on this. I know it's confusing sometimes. But I really see no reason to even be using this. There's no impeachment, there's no refreshing of recollection. Why are we reading this material? It is not relevant, it's not appropriate. Unless the witness is stumped or needs to be impeached, we don't need this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The most important thing is that you get it clear what you are putting to the witness. If you look at the transcript, we are dealing for a long time now just finding the relevant portion of the OTP statement. And this is really a waste of time. Perhaps a bad preparation of the cross-examination. I -- I would like to know which is the document on the screen at the moment, which is the number, as Mr. McCloskey was referring to a different number at the moment? Which one is it? Is it 65 ter 02064 still?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to emphasise both to you and Mr. McCloskey that I am the source of the confusion because I can't read or speak English. My legal assistant, who does speak and read English, is helping me. But from now on, because I have no intention of impeaching this witness, nor of checking what he said, I will just quote what I noted from today's transcript, because I'm not to be blamed for not speaking English. So I will leave alone this interview and I will focus on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Today, on page 34, line 14, of today's transcript, you discussed an encrypted telegram which contained an order that you should set up, as Mr. McCloskey said, a firing squad. And you explained how you received that telegram.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And how it was decoded while you were sleeping. As you remember that, my question is this: Did your duty organs, on the basis of the code that you had in the battalion, decode this telegram? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the telegram sent to you with the code that was used only by your Zvornik Brigade for communication in this manner?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were these intimate conversations between the brigade command and the subordinate units of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a table for decoding telegrams for a specific time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 34, from line 4 onwards, you talked about the numbers and letters used for the codes which are included in the tables. This is my question: Did every commanding officer in the battalion have training that would enable him to decode all the telegrams that would arrive to the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were. Each member of the battalion command should be trained in such a way that he can decode any possible encrypted telegram. I say that they should have been trained for that, but whether it was really like that or not, it's something I cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. On page 37, line 25, of today's transcript, Mr. McCloskey said that you contacted Popovic. And you reacted on page 38, line 3, and you said that you did not try to contact him but that you reached him accidentally and that he -- you got him on the phone through the duty operations officer. As you remember the situation, this is what I want to ask you. Mr. McCloskey asked you later on whether it was dark at the time and you said that you are not 100 percent sure?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the basis of all that, my question is this: What day was that, about which Mr. McCloskey asked you whether it was dark on that day or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do you know what date it was?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't ask me about any dates or days of the week. Because in all my previous statements, I said that if you want me to confirm what date or what day of the week it was, I am not certain, I do not remember, and if you insist, I might make an error. So as for the dates and the like, you don't have to ask me anything because I will tell you in advance that I'm not certain what day of the week or what specific date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you perhaps tell us whether it was on the 13th or on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes, but -- approximately, on the basis of everything else, it should have been these dates when these events took place in Rocevici, but I'm not certain and I cannot confirm whether it was on the 13th or 14th, when these unfortunate events happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you remember what was the date on which you received the telegram?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you that I don't remember any single date, and consequently, I would kindly ask you not to ask me such questions, if that's possible, questions that entail me saying exactly what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to apologise to you for asking you that, but I asked you that so that the Trial Chamber would have the information in the transcript, because earlier you talked about the arrival of the telegram and because there were other witnesses here who told us when approximately this could have happened, and you mentioned their names.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: They were talking about the fact that it happened around 2.00 after midnight?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So if it was the 12th, it actually the 13th, 2.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I think I was clear. I think I explained that. I spoke about the time in relation to the events in the field. I did not speak about some earlier period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have to look at page 17 of your second interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President requested me to tell exactly which interview that is. It's the 17th March of the year 2002. The interview was held in Banja Luka. And it's 65 ter 02063, page 17, lines 21 to 25. It's page 17 also in English, as my legal advisor just informed me. Thank you. So, everybody can see it, and I'm now going to read it and then I'll ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am quoting from the beginning of the sentence, page 17, line 20. You can follow it in Serbian. And in English, that's -- it's line 4 and onwards. I quote: "Well, first of all, we decided regardless of what was happening at the time, because we were expecting that somebody was going to do something because an order had been refused. But most of all we had in mind the fact that the previous day we saw on the television and we knew that it was General Mladic who announced to the public and everybody in Srebrenica that some sort of security would be guaranteed."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that you were able to follow in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We were not able to follow that. I didn't find it on that page. Please check if it's the right page. You said in English, it's line 4 and onwards. It is not line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do see on line 17 there's the -- a discussion where General Mladic is brought up. Perhaps that's where it begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance for the accused. But I would like to have -- to have it clear when the accused is asking for that document. Carry on, please, and put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. Thank you to Mr. McCloskey. I quoted what I knew. I knew that it was page 17 in Serbian. And I apologise for not giving the exact reference in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is as follows: First of all, do you remember what you stated here in this statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear this in the media, this thing that you mentioned, that General Mladic guaranteed the security and safety and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it on television after these events, much later. That's when you could see those things in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think. I think so, that's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But here in line 22, you say, and I quote: "The foremost fact in our mind was the fact that we saw it the day before on the television, and we knew that it was announced to the public and to everybody in Srebrenica that General Mladic guaranteed their safety." From this statement, it turns out that you saw it the day before, on the television. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer your question because it's -- I'm not clear about the question. I can't really see what this is all about and what is it that you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that what you said had been misinterpreted while this transcript was made and that it is different from what I have here as your statement?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. What you just read out to me, bearing in mind how you read it out, it means that I cannot really say anything about it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Without me reading out anything, why don't you read for yourself the whole sentence and then tell me whether you saw it on television or not.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. It is possible. Although I'm not sure about exactly when Srebrenica was taken over, it is possible that General Mladic gave some statements immediately after that and that in those statements he guaranteed the safety of the prisoners. So it is possible that we saw it the same night or whenever we watched television. So it is possible that this answer was given in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was that the basis for your decision?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because you say here: "We were expecting that something would be done about the fact that an order was refused."

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. We had completely different things in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You had completely different things in mind. Then why did you say here that General Mladic gave some guarantees to everybody in Srebrenica? My question was only about this specific point. Did you have in mind that fact?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things. It was an information. It was something that we knew. But apart from that, I, as a human being and a reserve officer, I would never allow myself or my associates to take part in such a mad idea of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you. But what I'm talking about here is, isn't that also similar to the public guarantees of security given by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really connect these two things. I don't know whether those things were taken into account or not. We are now talking about the time that had elapsed and if I were now to make a connection between these two things, it would be dishonest for me that I -- if I would say that I remember these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. But were you held responsible for the fact that you did not want take part in something that was illegal and something that was even completely ruled out as a possibility in public statements?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it realistic for you to refuse the order to execute soldiers, bearing in mind, that, in the media, you heard that the superior officers guaranteed the security and safety of those prisoners, saying that they would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really did not understand your question fully. I would rather not answer it. I'm not quite clear what exactly it is that you're asking. Could you maybe simplify your question? I'm definitely going to answer any question that you pose. But there is no need to quote anything or anybody else. Just ask me specifically, concretely, and I'm going to answer every question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Let us not quote anything, then. My question is: Could we say that you had some sort of guarantee that nobody would disturb you, because you heard in the media that everybody received guarantees that they were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I really did not think about that. If you think that, at the time I considered any guarantees, I have to tell you that probably, at that moment, I did not think about that. Really, I cannot give you an explanation about your question that would satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need anything here.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is, had you heard beforehand that there were guarantees of security to the population on television and on radio?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really telling you, here and now, that if I said something like that in 2001, that I had a recollection of this sort, that before these unfortunate events took place, and if I said that that happened after the takeover of Srebrenica, then, probably, yes, I did say something like that. But I can't remember these things that you are putting to me now. And I don't know whether it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are really running out of time. We need our second break. Before we do that, I have to make a correction. You, on page 71, line 12, you were referring to several pages of a document. That should read, to have it later on clear on the record, English page 17, lines 19 through 25 ; and B/C/S, not page 17 but page 18, lines 11 through 18. Just to clarify this situation on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a short question and then we will have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as a follow-up to the question put by the Defence, I would like to know, since you were a battalion commander, you had received a very important order. You were asked to send soldiers out to execute prisoners. This is not a standard order like going to fetch some bread. What I would like to know is this: In your army, as far as disciplinary matters are concerned, what sanctions were imposed when an officer like you refused to obey an order? More specifically, highly important orders stemming from these superiors in the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably in every army there are certain measures for refusing to obey an order. Bearing in mind what kind of order it was, I think that nobody was able, and nobody was in a position to start such a proceedings. That's my answer. On the other hand, truth be told, I can't tell you why such proceedings were not initiated. There is one reason. In relation to the Zvornik Brigade and the corps, there was nobody who could have initiated something like that, because everybody was running around in the command, in the brigade, everywhere. Nobody had enough courage in the brigade itself to stand up against such mad orders. Nobody, either in the brigade or in the corps. I think that those officers knew at the bottom of their souls that this was something abnormal, something crazy, something contrary to the times that we live in. I also think that that was one of the reasons why no disciplinary measures were taken against me. That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just have one question for you. You've testified in your evidence that you received a telegram requesting you to provide a platoon to undertake some executions. Do you know who -- who wrote you that telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already answered, and I am now repeating for the umpteenth time. When the telegram arrived, or, precisely, when I read the telegram, the contents of the telegram was so shocking for me, me and my associates, that, really, really, I'm now repeating it for I don't know which time, I did not remember the signature of the telegram. I may have read it, but then I was far more concentrated on the contents of the telegram, since I have already given some details about it. After the two telegrams that we have received, I said that Nikolic, who was security organ of the brigade, got in contact with me and tried, somehow, to force me to execute the order. So I think that I may have already answered your question, if I told you what I know, what I remember. So I think that that was maybe in the telegram as well. I sincerely hope that you will understand this statement of mine. And I'm going to say it once again. All the company commanders, or if they were absent, their deputies were informed about the contents of the telegram. I'm sure that many soldiers know about the contents, about the telegram. When I talk about soldiers, I talk about the soldiers of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. Now, why some individual cannot or do not want to remember these things, well, that's something entirely outside my powers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I have another question for you. How were you appointed to your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the order of the brigade commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Bosancic, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: What particular qualifications or skills or competences do you think influenced your appointment to these duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have in mind the military qualifications, I had none. What influenced Lieutenant-Colonel Bosancic? Maybe he had in mind the previous period when I performed the duty of the company commander. Probably, based on the way that I performed that duty, he considered that I was the best solution at that moment. I really cannot go any further into details right now about this topic because I was not the person thinking about it. It was somebody else who issued orders about it, and that somebody else had some information at his disposal, information about me. I think that the way that I performed my duties of the company commander in the 3rd Infantry Battalion may have acted as some sort of recommendation for my appointment as the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we, Mr. President, release Helge Brunborg. I see it's getting late and my voice is going out, and I'm not sure how much the General has to go. But it would be great to start with him tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is -- it is very unlikely that we can start with this witness. He should be released, it's my understanding as well. I think Mr. Tolimir has some more questions to go and there will be -- it has to be the opportunity for re-examination and some other questions, perhaps, from the Chamber. We must finally have now our second break and we will resume half past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to offer up a small apology because of erroneous references. Sometimes the lines of the transcript do not correspond the transcript we're using in the courtroom, and the documents that we used as working documents, some of them are in Word format, some of them are in PDF format, so then the order is not the same for some reason. We don't know why that happens, so we would like to apologise for all the difficulties that ensued because of this difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those kind words. I just want to give you a reason why this is really problematic. If the -- especially if the interpreters can't follow in the English or in the B/C/S version, and especially for us, we need the English or French translation, we need the clear reference. Otherwise additional translation problems will occur. And also for the court record it is also very difficult. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since a lot of time was spent on making the lines of the transcript correspond, so we used a lot of time on that, I would just like to process one more topic, and I would like to round off the previous topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since there were problems in establishing the exact date when this happened, I would like to ask you this: Are you saying that the prisoners were, first of all, captured and then they were deployed in your area? Is that something that is logical?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to see a statement by one witness. This is 9401. That is the transcript page, 9401, lines 1 to 12, where the witness, who is a Prosecution witness, and who had been captured, said that, on 13th, he was on the playground in Konjevic Polje. He described that General Mladic came to Konjevic Polje on that occasion, that he had a meeting with them, that he said that -- he would go for an exchange, that there were five people there whose names were listed, and that this took one hour. It took them one hour to make a list of people who were going to be exchanged. My question is: If all of this took place on the 13th, on the 13th at noon, then that prisoner probably would have been brought back on the 14th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, could that have been on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to give the floor to Mr. McCloskey before you put the next question. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, just on his -- General's paraphrase of the -- of the survivor witness, I believe he is speaking of the playground or the football pitch at Nova Kasaba. I'm not aware of a playground at Konjevic Polje. There is a building in Konjevic Polje but it's -- it's the playground, football pitch at Nova Kasaba, where I think, he is talking about the list and General Mladic. So I just wanted so sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I do agree with that. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Well, you have heard from the Prosecution and he remembers as well that this is something that the witness stated, that this happened at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba and that there, on the 13th, General Mladic appeared in the afternoon, that he gave them a speech, and that he took an hour to list the names of the people there. So my question is: If the prisoners were listed, on the 13th, as persons to be exchanged, could they have been located in Zvornik in the afternoon on the 13th, or was that some other day? Was it possible that they had spent the night in Bratunac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really unable to answer that question. I'm not familiar with the facts relating to those prisoners and a series of other circumstances dealing with those particular prisoners. I really would not venture into giving any kind of statement on that particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. You are a witness. This Court and I, as an accused, we need to establish the facts, the date when these prisoners were exchanged. You've already said that you don't want to do that. I understand why you don't want to do that and it's probably because you don't know. All I'm doing is asking you: Is it logical if somebody was arrested on the 13th but was placed in schools in the Zvornik municipality on the 12th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really would not want to say anything about that particular question, if you permit me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell me, can anyone be arrested a day after being placed in a particular area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat this question again? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This witness of the Prosecution that we mentioned said that on the 13th, he was on the football pitch and that his name was taken down and that General Mladic gave him a speech, that General Mladic said that they were going to be exchanged, that it took them an hour to make a list of these people, that this was something that was done by five people.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, all of that is fine. Just the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If they were on the pitch on the 13th, is there a possibility that on the 12th they were located in Zvornik? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: There's no logic to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we have pin-pointed that the 12th is being ruled out as a possible date. All right. Let's go on. If you remember, in your statement, you referred to someone telling you that there was an order issued from up high. The Prosecutor also said that. He didn't say who issued this order. Then we need to pin-point who that person could be or rule out somebody who could not have issued that order. Do you remember any possible persons who would fit that description?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we've seen now that on the 13th, General Mladic was on the football pitch, that this was something that was recorded by television, that he was making a list of the prisoners and this is something that the prisoners themselves testified to. And I have a statement here, D3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the basis of that, my question is: So, we don't know exactly who it was who issued that order; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd object. He needs to get his facts straight on this. There are hundreds of people at this soccer field. We have one prisoner that survived. There's not prisoners that I'm aware of that have given this evidence. There is one survivor. So to suggest that there's several prisoners providing this is inappropriate. He needs to keep his facts straight on these crucial issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the question? No, sorry, there was no -- there was not a question yet. Mr. Tolimir, please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question was, and I stopped because Mr. McCloskey was on his feet. The question was: If one survivor claimed that, on the 13th, he was on the football pitch, that there was a speech, that his name was written down, and that he was told that he would be going to -- for an exchange, would that indicate that on the 13th the position was to proceed with the exchange and to list the prisoners? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: How can I know what the position was? I did not have any kind of insight into that matter, in order to be able to say anything about that question. I wouldn't want to be dealing with any assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. All right. Just tell me, is there any logic in listing the prisoners for an exchange, to record them with cameras, to give them a speech, and then for that same person who was organising all of that would then have them killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I clearly stated exactly what I think about that particular issue. So as for logic, that is something that I would not really use anymore. I wouldn't use that term anymore, "logic." Had there been any logic in any of that, I wouldn't be here and you wouldn't be here either. Evidently somebody did not want, for whatever reasons, simply to -- well, actually, I really don't know what I could tell you about this question, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you for a moment. I have some doubt if the kind of questioning is -- helps you and your Defence in any way. The witness made very clear that he doesn't recall exact dates. Therefore, it's not helpful to put questions to that effect. And the other thing is, to -- to ask him about events he was not present and to draw some conclusions of different events, and if something is logical, this is a question you should answer yourself and everybody else in the courtroom, especially if it's related to events that the witness has never testified about. Please bear that in mind and put questions to the relevant parts of his previous testimony, and you should continue in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I understand you, and I understand the witness, too. But in order for us to establish the dates, all I can do is ask him whether, on the basis of the references given by the witness who survived, that he was in Kasaba on the 13th, is the witness able to say whether they were people who were prisoners in Nova Kasaba on the 13th. Thank you. I don't want anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I that I already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Could the e-court please show us D3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document on the screen. We spoke about the 13th, and this document talks about the 14th and the 15th. Can you please look at the second paragraph of this document. This is a statement by Major-General Elliott, a British Army general, an officer of the British Army. And in the second paragraph of the statement he says: "On July 14th, 1995, I travelled to Belgrade with Bildt, General de Lapresle and others ... Mr. Bildt attended a meeting with President Slobodan Milosevic of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia between approximately 1300 and 1700 hours. At the conclusion of this meeting, Mr. Bildt debriefed the other members of his delegation, including myself, on issues relating to his meeting with President Milosevic. Later that same evening, at ... 1900 hours, Mr. Bildt and General de Lapresle met with President Milosevic and General Ratko Mladic, commander of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army. The meeting concluded at approximately 2200 hours on the 14th of July, 1995." This was the first paragraph. In the second paragraph, line 4, the same person states: "On the 15th of July, 1995, in Belgrade, Mr. Bildt, Ambassador Stoltenberg, Mr. Akashi ... attended the meetings with President Milosevic and other members of his delegation. In attendance at his meeting was General Mladic. The meeting commenced at about 1200 hours and concluded at about 2200 hours. During this time, General Mladic remained in my presence until the conclusion of the meeting." So my question is: If the witness that survived says that General Mladic was in this place on the 13th and then he was where he is said to be on the 14th and the 15th, could General Mladic have been present at these locations that you referred to, the elementary school in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: This depends on the transport means that he had at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you quoted from paragraph 3, lines 1 through 7, and not second paragraph, line 4, just for the record, to have it clear what you are putting to the witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Should I repeat this quote? I have read the whole of the second paragraph and the third paragraph from the line 5 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you didn't read from the second paragraph but from the third paragraph. I just wanted to make it clear for the record. And now continue, please. Don't repeat anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I have to read the first paragraph because I want it to be in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are in the record. You were quoting absolutely correctly but you were reading from the second and the third paragraph. I think your -- Mr. Gajic will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now continue and put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, if General Mladic, on the 14th of July, 1995, had a meeting with Mr. Elliot and Mr. Bildt, and if, on the 15th of July, he had a meeting from 12.00 to 22 hours, could he have been at some other location at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like to tell you once again, I had no information about the whereabouts of General Mladic, about whom he met, when he met them. That is something that I know absolutely nothing about it. And I really cannot understand that are you now asking me to answer questions about such details since I have absolutely no idea about it. Excuse me. I certainly could not have had any such information, and now you expect me to talk about something that I know nothing about. I was not privy to such information. I think this is really inappropriate. You cannot ask me about such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you. I understand why you don't want to answer and I'm not going to insist on it. I read you a statement and a transcript of a witness who was in Nova Kasaba, but I understand why you don't want to answer whether somebody can be at two different places simultaneously. The Trial Chamber is going to decide about that, and I'm not going to ask you about this. I'm going to ask you about something that you maybe have some knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 2063. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We need 65 ter 2063, page 45 in Serbian, lines 3 to 8. And in English, it's page 44, lines 17 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is where you say that you had been warned about the attack that threatened the Zvornik Brigade on the part of the sabotage groups and the units leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about this event or whatever you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, we would receive information through telegram telling us that enemy armed columns were moving through the depth of our territory. By that, I mean behind our defence lines. Their possible axis of movement went through my zone of defence. The villages of Malesici and Boskovici. We received instructions to take certain measures so that our soldiers would be in the unit and alert, in order to prevent any sort of surprise, such as being ambushed from the back, or being attacked from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is as follows: Did the units of the 28th Division from Srebrenica move under fire through the zone of responsibility of your brigade with the intent to cross the zone of defence of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your brigade have any losses, bearing in mind that they were moving and taking part in action?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your battalion have any losses?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many losses did you have?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be sure about it. I think two soldiers, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any captured in this conflict, in this breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D373, page 3. Thank you. Yes, page 3. Now the last paragraph on this page bears number 3 in Serbian. In English, I think it's the following page. Thank you. So it's the third paragraph from the top, yes. So in English, it's at the top of the page, in Serbian it's at the bottom of the page, both paragraphs bearing number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It goes as follows: "The units of the 28th Division are pulling out of Srebrenica while still fighting. They have remained compact. They have scored success after success in the temporarily occupied territory. They have inflicted great losses on the aggressors. So far, they have eight Chetniks alive in captivity. Units of the 28th Division have linked up with the infiltrated units of the 2nd Corps. Their joint forces have continued fighting in the temporarily occupied territory. It is expected that they will fully link up with this unit. Activities are underway to exploit the success of units carrying out the breakthrough." So this is a document written by Rasim Delic. You can see in the English version that his name appears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now have the following page, the last page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that this was signed by Army General, Commander Rasim Delic. The report is dated the 16th of July, 1995. You can see that on the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So he informed other units within his army about it. You can see here the masthead towards the bottom of the page. My question is as follows: Was this attack as large as described here and was there a real danger that those compact forces which managed to leave Srebrenica would threaten units such as battalions along their path of breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He mentions eight captured Chetniks. Was there anybody captured in your unit?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what do you know in general about this fighting and were there any captured people?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never in those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know how many captured or killed members of the brigade were there in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know any precise data. I really wouldn't dare say anything about it. Right now, these data are not available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember which unit from the brigade took part in prevention of this breakthrough of the enemy through the zone of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Probably all the units of the Zvornik Brigade took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, through the territory of which battalion did the Muslim formation accomplish its breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the direction of the village of Kitovnica, but I'm not sure. I'm not sure about which battalion had this village in its zone of responsibility. I think it was the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know which battalion defended the area of Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 4th Battalion. I'm not quite sure about what was the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade in that area, so I'm not exactly sure about in which zone of defence which village was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Delic here says that the units of the 20th Division left Srebrenica while fighting. My question is as follows: Did the Serbian army open a corridor for them, resulting in the fact that there were not other casualties in that particular zone?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: A corridor was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look at the clock, we are past 7.00 already. We have to stop it now. And we are in a difficult position. You have nearly used two hours for your cross-examination. Some parts, as we discussed earlier, was a waste of time because figuring out the right documents with the right numbers. I don't know how to continue. Can you tell me what is your estimation, how much time do you need to finalise your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We announced two hours. We have spent two hours so far, so I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, that's not true. That's not true. You said one to two hours. This is different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. So if we use two hours, then I finished the cross-examination. I would like to thank the witness for his answers, and I wish you safe journey home on behalf of the Defence. May God bless him and may he continue his life in joy and happiness. Thank you, Your Honour, and to everybody helping us, to everybody watching this trial. Thank you to the Registry. And I apologise for any technical difficulties while using the transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was not the transcript what was the problem but the OTP interviews, and they are in both languages for a long time at your disposal. This is the problem. Mr. McCloskey, what is the situation according to re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, this concludes your examination in this trial. Thank you that we -- you were able to come to The Hague again and to help us to find out the truth, and thank you for your assistance you were able to provide. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the Chamber would like to thank you again. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. Thank you, and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
